questions.stem: Which of the following best defines self-regulation?
options: A business or industry setting and monitoring its own standards rather than being required to by law
Regulation imposed by the host country's government
Regulation agreed between two governments
Monitoring of a business by its customers
questions.why: It is faster and more flexible than legislation, and voluntary and unenforceable.
whyNot: That is legal control.
That is an international agreement.
That is consumer pressure.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines regulatory arbitrage?
options: Locating activity in the country with the least demanding rules
Settling a dispute between two regulators
Complying with the strictest rules in every country
Challenging a regulation in court
questions.why: It is one of the three consequences of MNCs being global while laws are national.
whyNot: That is regulatory dispute resolution.
That is the opposite approach.
That is litigation.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a boycott?
options: An organised refusal to buy a business's products to force a change in its behaviour
A government ban on trade with a country
A refusal by workers to perform their duties
A decision by a business to leave a market
questions.why: It goes straight to revenue, which is the language a business responds to fastest.
whyNot: That is an embargo.
That is a strike.
That is a market exit.

questions.stem: What is the structural problem in controlling MNCs?
options: MNCs are global while laws are national
MNCs are always larger than governments
MNCs are exempt from national law
No country wishes to regulate them
questions.why: A company can locate profit, production and ownership wherever suits it while no single government has authority over the whole group.
whyNot: Some are very large, but not all exceed government scale.
They are subject to the law of each country they operate in.
Many countries regulate them actively.

questions.stem: What is the mechanism through which an MNC's power operates?
options: The threat to relocate, which does not have to be exercised to be effective
Direct control of the host government's budget
The power to change national laws unilaterally
Ownership of the country's currency
questions.why: Where the investment is genuinely mobile the power is real; where it is tied to a resource or an immovable asset it is far weaker.
whyNot: Governments control their own budgets.
Laws are made by governments, though lobbying shapes them.
Currency is issued by central banks.

questions.stem: Which operation gives a government the most leverage over an MNC?
options: A mine or a resort, because the asset cannot be moved
An assembly plant with standard equipment
A customer service centre
A software development office
questions.why: Asking how mobile the operation is should be the first step in any answer about controlling MNCs.
whyNot: Assembly is relatively mobile.
Service centres are highly mobile.
Software work is highly mobile.

questions.stem: How does political influence usually affect regulation?
options: Laws are shaped, delayed or diluted before they are passed rather than broken
Laws are routinely repealed at a company's request
Companies are given the power to write legislation
Regulators are legally required to consult only businesses
questions.why: Lobbying, industry associations and providing expertise to governments drafting regulation are the usual channels.
whyNot: Repeal on request is not how it works.
Legislatures pass laws; businesses may provide input.
Consultation normally extends beyond business.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a strength of legal control?
options: It is binding and applies to every firm equally, so it does not disadvantage the ethical one
It applies beyond the country's borders in all cases
It can be introduced faster than business models change
It requires no enforcement capacity
questions.why: Enforceability through the courts with meaningful penalties is what distinguishes law from voluntary codes.
whyNot: It reaches only within national borders, except where extraterritorial law applies.
Regulation takes years while business models change in months.
Inspectors, courts and technical expertise are all required.

questions.stem: Against which type of business is consumer pressure least effective?
options: A business with no consumer brand, such as a component manufacturer
A high-street retailer
A branded food manufacturer
A consumer electronics company
questions.why: Reputation is a large part of the value of a consumer brand, so the threat is only credible where such a brand exists.
whyNot: Retailers are highly exposed to consumer pressure.
Branded manufacturers are highly exposed.
Consumer electronics brands are highly exposed.

questions.stem: Why can a boycott harm the workers it intends to help?
options: Cutting orders cuts their income without improving their conditions
Workers are legally liable for lost sales
Boycotts are usually directed at employees
Boycotts raise local prices for workers
questions.why: This is the same objection as withdrawing from a supplier, and it is worth naming in an evaluation.
whyNot: Workers carry no such liability.
They are directed at the business.
Price effects are not the main mechanism.

questions.stem: Why has social media changed the balance of control?
options: Evidence can be published instantly by anyone, so a local problem cannot stay local
It allows governments to enforce laws across borders
It guarantees the accuracy of allegations
It replaces the need for legal regulation
questions.why: Its weaknesses are equally real: accuracy is not guaranteed and attention fades before change is delivered.
whyNot: Enforcement still depends on legal jurisdiction.
Accuracy is one of its main weaknesses.
It supplements rather than replaces regulation.

questions.stem: Which mechanism shifts enforcement from the weakest jurisdiction to the strongest?
options: Home-country legislation with extraterritorial reach, such as anti-bribery and modern slavery laws
Self-regulation by the industry
Consumer boycotts in the host country
A pressure group campaign
questions.why: It is the only structural answer to regulatory arbitrage and the most sophisticated point available in this topic.
whyNot: Self-regulation is voluntary and unenforceable.
Host-country consumer pressure is often weak.
Campaigns have no legal authority.

questions.stem: What does international agreement on a minimum corporate tax rate attack?
options: The benefit of shifting reported profit to low-tax countries
The ability of MNCs to employ local workers
The freedom of MNCs to advertise internationally
The right of MNCs to repatriate profit
questions.why: It attacks transfer pricing directly, and it illustrates that controlling a global company requires governments to act together rather than compete.
whyNot: Employment is not affected.
Advertising is governed separately.
Repatriation is not restricted by tax agreements.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a strength of self-regulation?
options: It can apply across a whole group in every country at once, which no national law can
It is legally enforceable through the courts
It is monitored by independent regulators as standard
It sets more demanding standards than legislation
questions.why: It also uses the company's own expertise about what is practicable and can pre-empt regulation the industry would like even less.
whyNot: It is voluntary and unenforceable.
Monitoring is usually by the company or auditors it pays.
Standards set by those they apply to tend to be undemanding.

questions.stem: What is the fair judgement on self-regulation?
options: Necessary because it reaches where the law cannot, and insufficient because nothing compels compliance
Entirely worthless, because it is voluntary
Wholly adequate, because businesses know their own operations
Illegal in most jurisdictions
questions.why: It works best where an industry's reputation is collectively at stake and where codes are independently verified.
whyNot: It reaches across a whole group in a way no national law can.
Standards are set by those they apply to, so they tend to be weak.
It is lawful and widely used.

questions.stem: What determines how much control over MNCs is actually achievable?
options: The mobility of the investment and the strength of the host country's institutions
The size of the MNC's advertising budget
The number of countries the MNC operates in
Whether the MNC is publicly listed
questions.why: Where a weak state competes for mobile investment, control has to come from outside: home-country legislation, consumer pressure in its main markets, and international agreement.
whyNot: Advertising spend is not the relevant variable.
Geographic spread is not the determining factor.
Listing status affects disclosure rather than control.

questions.stem: Why do the mechanisms for controlling MNCs need to work together?
options: Law sets a floor, social media and pressure groups supply information, and consumer pressure makes reputation financial
Each mechanism is fully effective on its own
Only legal control has any effect
Only consumer pressure has any effect
questions.why: Self-regulation then reaches the parts of a global group that no regulator can, so no single mechanism is adequate.
whyNot: Each has clear limitations.
Law is limited by jurisdiction and enforcement capacity.
Consumer pressure is limited to branded businesses.
